## Overview

This study compares estimators of the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) in five synthetic panel families: classic factors, weak factors, mixed factors, sparse synthetic controls, and autoregressive outcomes. Each canonical panel contains 160 never-treated units, 40 treated units, 40 pre-treatment periods, and 10 post-treatment periods. All treated units adopt in the first post-treatment period. Their treatment effects increase from 0.2 to 2.0, which gives a true ATT of 1.1.

The estimators reconstruct untreated post-treatment outcomes in three ways. An outcome-model estimator uses a fitted untreated-outcome surface. Unit balancing weights control units so their pre-treatment outcomes match the treated units. Double balancing combines those donor weights with weights on pre-treatment periods in an augmented difference-in-differences score. The experiments vary factor-loading overlap, factor strength, donor sparsity, persistence, and integration to change which source of information is useful. For copyable construction code and `matshow` visualizations of every underlying design, start with the [Balancing DGP catalog](../canonical-designs.qmd).

The estimator ranking changes across these designs. Unit balancing is competitive in several good-overlap and synthetic-control settings. Double balancing has substantially lower RMSE under poor factor-loading overlap and persistent integrated dynamics. No outcome model or balancing configuration minimizes RMSE in every design.

The reproduction uses three validation standards:

1. On the same fixed panel, the R quadratic-program reference and `crabbymetrics.AugmentedBalancing` agree to numerical precision across 48 estimator configurations.
2. On a second fixed panel, Python FE, IFE, MCPanel, generalized synthetic-control, and panel-VAR surfaces agree with their R reference surfaces within specified cell tolerances.
3. Independent R and Python Monte Carlo runs compare the full 398-cell slide grid. Differences are reported in units of combined Monte Carlo standard errors.

Of the 398 Monte Carlo cells, 390 are within three combined Monte Carlo standard errors. Every FE, IFE, generalized synthetic-control, and VAR cell is within that boundary. The eight exceptions consist of five correlated MCPanel cells in the poor-overlap classic-factor setting and three ARIMA cells in the low-persistence time-series settings. These two outcome-model-specific patterns are documented below.

```{python}
max_standardized = comparison["standardized_difference"].abs().max()
within_three = int(comparison["within_three_mcse"].sum())
summary_claims = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "check": [
            "Same-panel estimator cases",
            "Same-panel outcome-model surfaces",
            "Matched Monte Carlo cells",
            "Cells within three combined MCSE",
            "R replications per matched cell",
            "Python replications per matched cell",
            "Largest absolute standardized RMSE difference",
        ],
        "result": [
            48,
            5,
            len(comparison),
            within_three,
            200,
            200,
            f"{max_standardized:.3f}",
        ],
    }
)
summary_claims
```

## Sources and implementation contracts

The visual reference is `drafts/slides.pdf`, with source in `overleaf_v2/acic_2024_deck.tex`. The executable contracts come from:

- `code/ziyi/formal simulation DGP.R` for panel generation;
- `code/ziyi/classic_did_framework.R` for estimator composition;
- `code/ziyi/support/sdid_unit.R` and `sdid_time.R` for ridge balancing;
- `code/ziyi/support/scm.R` for the penalized-SCM donor loss;
- `output/simulation/*/estimation.RData` for the exact slide Monte Carlo draws; and
- `code/apoorva/00_acic_tabfig.R` for the slide aggregation rule, $\operatorname{RMSE}=\sqrt{\operatorname{mean}(\widehat\tau-\tau)^2}$.

The reproduced ATT heatmaps appear on deck pages 27-28 for classic factors, 33-36 for synthetic controls, 41-44 for time series, 48-49 for weak factors, and 54-55 for mixed factors.

The Python comparison is exact for the balancing estimator and its penalties. It also implements all outcome-model columns in the R heatmaps: FE, IFE, MCPanel, generalized synthetic control, panel VAR, and the time-series-only ARIMA column. The Monte Carlo comparison uses the same probability laws and replication indices 1 through 200, but NumPy and R do not use the same seeded random streams. Therefore, Monte Carlo equality is evaluated relative to simulation uncertainty, not bitwise equality.

Several details in the executable R source determine the numerical results:

| Component | Executable R contract | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Factor scale | Divide each realized factor path by its sample SD | Fixes the realized signal scale and signal-to-noise ratio |
| Synthetic donors | Sample active donors without replacement with weights 1 for favored donors and 0.1 for other donors | Changes the donor support in each replication |
| Time-series mean | Set the treated innovation mean to 0.25 | Separates the innovation mean from the unconditional AR level mean |
| Mixed factors | Generate two half-panels and restart the seed for the second half | Preserves the dependence structure of the archived experiment |
| Unit balancing | Use optimized unit weights and uniform pre-period weights in the augmented score | Retains the time correction when time weights are not optimized |
| Period targets | Fit one time-weight vector for each post period | Allows the time target to change over the post-treatment path |
| IFE controls | Rank 2 and force 3; tolerance $10^{-5}$ for classic and weak factors and $10^{-4}$ otherwise | Matches the archived `fect` calls |
| MCPanel | Unit and time effects with fixed nuclear-norm penalty 0.002 | Matches `lambda_L=0.002` with cross-validation disabled |
| Panel VAR | Use 2 lags for classic and weak factors, 1 for mixed factors and SCM, and 4 for time-series panels | The archived scripts do not use one common lag order |
| ARIMA | Fit an automatic univariate time-series model to each unit | This column appears only in the time-series DGP |
| Monte Carlo size | Use 200 successful replications per cell | Makes the reported RMSE comparable to the archived R experiment |

These are part of the statistical specification. They are not interchangeable implementation details.

## Exact same-panel estimator parity

The fixture generator in `crabbymetrics/tests/fixtures/generate_r_augmented_balancing_reference.R` uses R and `quadprog` to fit all combinations of:

- `balance`: unit, time, or double;
- `unit_target`: cohort or individual;
- `time_target`: all post periods or one post period at a time;
- `balance_on`: raw outcomes or outcome-model residuals; and
- `unit_loss`: SDID ridge or penalized SCM.

The following code sends the identical panel and outcome-model surface to Python.

```{python}
fixture_dir = VIGNETTE / "reference"
panel_fixture = np.genfromtxt(
    fixture_dir / "r_augmented_balancing_panel.csv",
    delimiter=",",
    names=True,
)
n_units = int(panel_fixture["unit"].max()) + 1
n_periods = int(panel_fixture["period"].max()) + 1
y_fixture = panel_fixture["outcome"].reshape(n_units, n_periods)
w_fixture = panel_fixture["treatment"].reshape(n_units, n_periods)
m_fixture = panel_fixture["outcome_model"].reshape(n_units, n_periods)

with (fixture_dir / "r_augmented_balancing_results.csv").open(newline="") as stream:
    r_cases = list(csv.DictReader(stream))

parity_rows = []
for case in r_cases:
    model = cm.AugmentedBalancing(
        balance=case["balance"],
        unit_target=case["unit_target"],
        time_target=case["time_target"],
        balance_on=case["balance_on"],
        unit_loss=case["unit_loss"],
        unit_penalty=float(case["unit_penalty"]),
        max_iterations=10_000,
    )
    model.fit(y_fixture, w_fixture, m_fixture)
    python_att = float(model.summary()["att"])
    parity_rows.append(
        {
            "balance": case["balance"],
            "unit target": case["unit_target"],
            "time target": case["time_target"],
            "fit weights on": case["balance_on"],
            "unit loss": case["unit_loss"],
            "R ATT": float(case["att"]),
            "Python ATT": python_att,
            "absolute difference": abs(python_att - float(case["att"])),
        }
    )

parity = pd.DataFrame(parity_rows)
assert len(parity) == 48
assert parity["absolute difference"].max() < 1e-8
parity.sort_values("absolute difference", ascending=False).head(8)
```

The maximum absolute ATT difference is:

```{python}
f"{parity['absolute difference'].max():.3e}"
```

This is numerical parity. It is separate from the Monte Carlo comparison.

### Same-panel outcome-model parity

The R fixture in `scripts/export_r_outcome_model_reference.R` fits FE, fixed-rank IFE, MCPanel, generalized synthetic control, and panel VAR to one deterministic panel. The Python functions below receive the same outcome and treatment matrices.

```{python}
outcome_panel = pd.read_csv(VIGNETTE / "reference" / "r_outcome_model_panel.csv")
outcome_reference = pd.read_csv(VIGNETTE / "reference" / "r_outcome_model_surfaces.csv")
n_outcome_units = int(outcome_panel["unit"].max()) + 1
n_outcome_periods = int(outcome_panel["period"].max()) + 1
outcome_fixture = outcome_panel["outcome"].to_numpy().reshape(
    n_outcome_units, n_outcome_periods
)
treatment_fixture = outcome_panel["treatment"].to_numpy().reshape(
    n_outcome_units, n_outcome_periods
)

outcome_functions = {
    "fe": two_way_fe_surface,
    "ife": interactive_fixed_effects_surface,
    "MCPanel": mcpanel_surface,
    "gsynth": generalized_synthetic_control_surface,
    "VAR": panel_var_surface,
}
outcome_parity_rows = []
for model_name, function in outcome_functions.items():
    reference_surface = (
        outcome_reference[outcome_reference["model"].eq(model_name)]["counterfactual"]
        .to_numpy()
        .reshape(n_outcome_units, n_outcome_periods)
    )
    python_surface = function(outcome_fixture, treatment_fixture)
    outcome_parity_rows.append(
        {
            "outcome model": model_name,
            "maximum absolute cell difference": np.max(
                np.abs(python_surface - reference_surface)
            ),
        }
    )
outcome_parity = pd.DataFrame(outcome_parity_rows)
assert outcome_parity.loc[
    ~outcome_parity["outcome model"].eq("MCPanel"),
    "maximum absolute cell difference",
].max() < 1e-8
assert outcome_parity.loc[
    outcome_parity["outcome model"].eq("MCPanel"),
    "maximum absolute cell difference",
].max() < 5e-4
outcome_parity
```

The MCPanel cell tolerance is $5\times10^{-4}$ because the R and Rust SVD solvers stop after slightly different relative-objective updates. FE, IFE, generalized synthetic control, and VAR use a $10^{-8}$ cell tolerance. ARIMA is checked by its API and Monte Carlo contracts because the historical `fable` version is not installed in this environment.

## R and Python Monte Carlo results

### Plot construction

Each row below contains the complete R heatmap and the complete Python heatmap for one setting. The two panels have the same rows, columns, blanks, and color scale. The slide aggregation leaves unit-only and unaugmented double balancing blank outside the FE column because those two estimators do not use an outcome model.

Color follows the slide rule: direct RMSE from 0 to 3 on the reversed Spectral palette. Values above 3 and unavailable cells are gray. Printed labels retain the uncensored RMSE values.

```{python}
def _matrix_for(data, setting, outcomes):
    selected = data[data["setting"].eq(setting)]
    matrix = (
        selected.pivot_table(index="frame", columns="outcome", values="rmse", aggfunc="first")
        .reindex(index=FRAME_ORDER, columns=outcomes)
    )
    matrix.loc[["u-balance", "d-balance"], [name for name in outcomes if name != "fe"]] = np.nan
    return matrix


def _draw_heatmap(ax, matrix, title, *, show_y=True):
    values = matrix.to_numpy(dtype=float)
    color_values = np.ma.masked_where(
        ~np.isfinite(values) | (values < 0) | (values > 3),
        values,
    )
    palette = mpl.colormaps["Spectral_r"].copy()
    palette.set_bad("#8c8c8c")
    image = ax.imshow(
        color_values,
        aspect="auto",
        cmap=palette,
        vmin=0,
        vmax=3,
    )
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10, loc="left")
    ax.set_xticks(range(matrix.shape[1]), matrix.columns, rotation=35, ha="right")
    if show_y:
        ax.set_yticks(range(matrix.shape[0]), matrix.index)
    else:
        ax.set_yticks(range(matrix.shape[0]), [])
    for row in range(values.shape[0]):
        for column in range(values.shape[1]):
            value = values[row, column]
            if np.isfinite(value):
                ax.text(column, row, f"{value:.3g}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)
    return image


def plot_family(family, settings, title):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(
        len(settings),
        2,
        figsize=(15.5, max(3.4, 3.2 * len(settings))),
        gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1]},
        squeeze=False,
        constrained_layout=True,
    )
    for row, setting in enumerate(settings):
        r_setting = r_results[(r_results["family"] == family) & (r_results["setting"] == setting)]
        available = [name for name in OUTCOME_ORDER if name in set(r_setting["outcome"])]
        r_full = _matrix_for(r_setting, setting, available)
        p_setting = python_results[
            (python_results["family"] == family) & (python_results["setting"] == setting)
        ]
        p_full = _matrix_for(p_setting, setting, available)
        image = _draw_heatmap(
            axes[row, 0],
            r_full,
            f"R reference | {setting}",
            show_y=True,
        )
        _draw_heatmap(
            axes[row, 1],
            p_full,
            f"Python reproduction | {setting}",
            show_y=False,
        )
    fig.colorbar(
        image,
        ax=axes,
        orientation="horizontal",
        fraction=0.025,
        pad=0.08,
        label="RMSE (values above 3 are gray)",
    )
    fig.suptitle(title, fontsize=14)
    plt.show()
```

### Unit and double balancing in difficult designs

The following table isolates four settings in which double balancing reduces RMSE relative to unit balancing. Ratios above one favor double balancing.

```{python}
ranking_cases = [
    ("classic_factor", "NN=200;a=1", "Classic factor, poor overlap"),
    ("weak_factor", "NN=200;a=1", "Weak factor, poor overlap"),
    ("mixed_factor", "NN=200;a=1", "Mixed factor, poor overlap"),
    ("time_series", "NN=200;a=0.9;I=1", "Integrated AR, phi=0.9"),
]

ranking_rows = []
for family, setting, label in ranking_cases:
    for language, data, value_column in [
        ("R", comparison, "r_rmse"),
        ("Python", comparison, "python_rmse"),
    ]:
        selected = data[(data["family"] == family) & (data["setting"] == setting)]
        unit = float(selected.loc[selected["frame"] == "u-balance", value_column].iloc[0])
        double = float(selected.loc[selected["frame"] == "d-balance", value_column].iloc[0])
        ranking_rows.append(
            {
                "DGP": label,
                "language": language,
                "unit-only RMSE": unit,
                "double RMSE": double,
                "unit/double ratio": unit / double,
            }
        )
pd.DataFrame(ranking_rows).round(3)
```

## Between-language Monte Carlo agreement

For independent Monte Carlo estimates $\widehat r_R$ and $\widehat r_P$, define

$$
z_{R-P}=\frac{\widehat r_P-\widehat r_R}
{\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\widehat r_P)^2+
\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\widehat r_R)^2}}.
$$

For errors $e_s$ and $r=\sqrt{S^{-1}\sum_s e_s^2}$, the delta-method standard error used here is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(r)=
\frac{\operatorname{sd}(e_s^2)}{2r\sqrt{S}}.
$$

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.5), constrained_layout=True)
ordered = comparison.sort_values("standardized_difference")
colors = ordered["family"].astype("category").cat.codes

ax.axhline(-3, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.axhline(0, color="0.5", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Matched RMSE cell, ordered by standardized difference")
ax.set_ylabel("Python minus R, in combined MCSE units")
ax.set_title("R and Python RMSE differences relative to combined Monte Carlo uncertainty", loc="left")
plt.show()
```

### Discrepancy diagnosis

The same-panel checks identify the source of a difference before the Monte Carlo results are interpreted:

- FE, IFE, generalized synthetic control, and panel VAR agree cell by cell to $10^{-8}$. A Monte Carlo difference in these columns is not an estimator-algebra difference.
- MCPanel agrees to $5\times10^{-4}$ on the fixed panel. Its remaining numerical difference comes from the stopping sequence used by the Rcpp and Rust SVD routines.
- ARIMA does not have a same-panel historical-`fable` fixture. The Python search contains the true DGP models but searches fewer ARMA specifications than `fable::ARIMA`. A persistent ARIMA-column difference is therefore an outcome-model search difference.
- The R and Python simulations use independent random streams. The standardized difference accounts for the reported Monte Carlo error from both runs.
- Cells in one setting reuse the same 200 panels. Their standardized differences are correlated, so a cluster of adjacent cells is one setting-level diagnostic rather than a set of independent tests.

A standardized difference near zero is expected under the common probability law. The two tables above show both the most extreme cells and the outcome-model-level pattern. This makes a package-algorithm difference visible instead of attributing every difference to random simulation noise.

## `pypanelsim` simulation API

`pypanelsim` is a separate estimator-neutral package with NumPy and Matplotlib as its runtime dependencies. This documentation environment installs crabbymetrics only through the optional `docs` extra. The simulation package itself does not import crabbymetrics or contain the outcome-model estimators used later in this report.

The simulation pipeline separates four required objects and one optional shared-feature stage:

| Abstraction | Contract |
|---|---|
| `PanelDimensions` | Defines only the rectangular `(n_units, n_periods)` shape |
| Unit-feature model | Optionally draws observed covariates and latent unit factors before assignment |
| Assignment model | Returns binary treatment; built-ins support fixed, randomized, sigmoid-selected, and generalized-propensity cohort assignment |
| Outcome model | Returns untreated outcomes conditional on dimensions and realized treatment |
| Effect model | Returns realized effects that are zero outside treated cells |
| `PanelSimulator` | Composes the three components and returns a validated `PanelDataset` |

The component interfaces use structural typing. A new design can provide a plain class with the documented `assign()` or `generate()` method without inheriting from a package base class. Randomness enters through an explicit NumPy generator shared in pipeline order.

```{python}
for object_ in [
    PanelDimensions,
    PanelSimulator,
    GaussianUnitFeatures,
    SingleCohortAssignment,
    RandomizedSingleCohortAssignment,
    BinaryLogitAssignment,
    StaggeredAdoption,
    GeneralizedPropensityAssignment,
    ConstantEffect,
    LinearRampEffect,
]:
    print(object_.__name__, inspect.signature(object_))
```

### Common data contract

```{python}
print(inspect.signature(CanonicalPanelConfig))
print(inspect.signature(PanelDataset))
```

`CanonicalPanelConfig` has six fields:

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| `n_control` | 160 | Number of never-treated units |
| `n_treated` | 40 | Number of treated units |
| `n_pre` | 40 | Number of pre-treatment periods |
| `n_post` | 10 | Number of post-treatment periods |
| `effect_slope` | 0.2 | Increase in the treatment effect per post period |
| `noise_variance` | 0.36 | Variance of the common idiosyncratic error |

Every generator returns an immutable `PanelDataset` object. The canonical factories order controls first, but the generic simulation contract does not require that order. Arrays have shape `(n_units, n_periods)`.

| Attribute | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `outcome` | Observed $Y=Y(0)+\tau D$ |
| `untreated_outcome` | Latent $Y(0)$ |
| `treatment` | Absorbing treatment matrix |
| `treatment_effect` | Cell-level effect matrix |
| `control_units`, `treated_units` | Integer row indices |
| `adoption_times` | Unit-specific first-treatment positions; never-treated units use the panel horizon |
| `name` | DGP identifier |
| `metadata` | Read-only components such as factors, loadings, paths, and donor weights |
| `unit_covariates`, `unit_covariate_names` | Observed time-invariant assignment features available to estimators |
| `true_att` | Mean effect over treated cells; 1.1 under the canonical design |

`as_arrays()` returns the standard wide outcome and treatment matrices for a downstream estimator. `as_long_dict()` returns flat unit, time, outcome, treatment, untreated-outcome, and treatment-effect columns for pandas, Polars, or Arrow without adding those libraries as simulation dependencies. Both return read-only data by default; `copy=True` requests writable copies.

```{python}
canonical = classic_factor(overlap=1.0, seed=17)
print(canonical.outcome.shape)
print(canonical.true_att)
print(sorted(canonical.metadata))
print([array.shape for array in canonical.as_arrays()])
```

### Generator signatures

```{python}
generators = [
    classic_factor,
    weak_factor,
    mixed_factor,
    synthetic_control,
    time_series,
    factor_synthetic,
]
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "function": [function.__name__ for function in generators],
        "signature": [str(inspect.signature(function)) for function in generators],
    }
)
```

### Canonical settings

The canonical functions are concise one-draw wrappers around reusable simulator factories. Named creation is also available through the package registry.

```{python}
print(available_canonical_designs())
simulator = make_canonical("classic_factor", overlap=1.0)
print(inspect.signature(classic_factor_design))
print(simulator)
```

| Function | Main setting parameter | Slide settings | Executable-source contract |
|---|---|---|---|
| `classic_factor` | `overlap` | 0, 1 | Two standardized drift factors; loading means $-a$ for controls and $a$ for treated units |
| `weak_factor` | `overlap` | 0, 1 | Five drift and five cyclical factors, each with sample SD 0.2 |
| `mixed_factor` | `overlap` | 0, 1 | One 100-unit drift half-panel with all treated units and one 100-control cyclical half-panel; both restart the seed |
| `synthetic_control` | `active_share` | 0.1, 0.5 | Equal active weights; favored donors have sampling weight 1 and other donors 0.1 |
| `time_series` | `coefficient`, `integrated` | $\phi\in\{0.2,0.9\}$, $I\in\{0,1\}$ | Treated innovation mean 0.25; control innovation mean 0 |
| `factor_synthetic` | `overlap` | archived mixture | Equal mixture of factor and SCM components; retained for the archived experiment output |

The slide prose and executable R source differ in three places. The library follows the executable source because that source generated the stored results:

- Factors are divided by their realized sample standard deviation, not by fixed constants 7.5 and 0.7.
- Synthetic active donors are sampled with unequal probabilities, not selected as the exact top set.
- The AR function receives innovation mean 0.25. It does not receive recursion intercept $0.25/(1-\phi)$.

### Custom dimensions

```{python}
small = CanonicalPanelConfig(n_control=24, n_treated=6, n_pre=20, n_post=5)
draw = synthetic_control(active_share=0.25, config=small, seed=203)
print(draw.outcome.shape)
print(draw.metadata["outcome"]["active_donors"])
print(draw.metadata["outcome"]["donor_weights"].sum())
```

The Python `seed` contract is reproducibility within Python. It is not a claim that NumPy seed 203 equals R seed 203 cell by cell.

For repeated experiments, `PanelSimulator.iter_simulations(replications, seed=...)` uses child `SeedSequence` streams. This avoids treating adjacent integer seeds as the independence mechanism. The reproduction keeps the original integer replication indices because they are part of the archived R comparison contract.

## Outcome-model reproduction API

The functions in `scripts/outcome_models.py` accept two same-shaped NumPy arrays. `outcome` contains units in rows and periods in columns. `treatment` is a binary, absorbing-treatment matrix. Each function returns a finite array of the same shape that estimates the untreated-outcome surface. A function never uses a treated post-treatment outcome as an observed response during fitting.

```{python}
outcome_model_functions = [
    two_way_fe_surface,
    interactive_fixed_effects_surface,
    mcpanel_surface,
    generalized_synthetic_control_surface,
    panel_var_surface,
    arima_surface,
]
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "function": [function.__name__ for function in outcome_model_functions],
        "signature": [str(inspect.signature(function)) for function in outcome_model_functions],
    }
)
```

| Function | R column | Statistical operation | Archived experiment settings |
|---|---|---|---|
| `two_way_fe_surface` | `fe` | Alternating projection on additive unit and period effects over untreated cells | No tuning parameter |
| `interactive_fixed_effects_surface` | `ife` | Missing-cell EM with a rank-constrained interactive fixed-effects M-step | Rank 2, force 3; family-specific tolerance and iteration budget |
| `mcpanel_surface` | `MCPanel` | Nuclear-norm matrix completion with additive unit and period effects | `lambda_l=0.002`, tolerance $10^{-5}$, 1,000 iterations |
| `generalized_synthetic_control_surface` | `gsynth` | Estimate common factors on never-treated controls, then estimate treated loadings on pre-treatment data | Rank 2, force 3 |
| `panel_var_surface` | `VAR` | Pooled autoregression with additive unit and period effects, followed by recursive treated-unit forecasts | Lag orders 2, 2, 1, 1, and 4 by DGP family |
| `arima_surface` | `arima` | Select a univariate autoregression or integrated autoregression for each unit, then forecast treated periods | Conditional AIC; integration order 0 or 1; AR order 0 through 2 |

The family-specific runner settings are:

| DGP family | IFE tolerance | IFE maximum iterations | VAR lags |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Classic factor | $10^{-5}$ | 2,000 | 2 |
| Weak factor | $10^{-5}$ | 2,000 | 2 |
| Mixed factor | $10^{-4}$ | 4,000 | 1 |
| Synthetic control | $10^{-4}$ | 4,000 | 1 |
| Time series | $10^{-4}$ | 4,000 | 4 |

`panel_var_surface` sets the first $p$ fitted periods to zero, as the R code does after predictions with unavailable lags. For a treated unit, its first post-treatment prediction uses observed pre-treatment lags. Later predictions use earlier counterfactual predictions recursively.

The ARIMA function has a narrower automatic model search than the historical `fable::ARIMA` call. It includes the true AR(1) and ARIMA(1,1,0) laws used by the DGP, but it does not search moving-average or seasonal terms. The Monte Carlo comparison therefore reports the ARIMA column separately from the same-input parity tests.

## `crabbymetrics.AugmentedBalancing` API

### Constructor and fit

```{python}
print(inspect.signature(cm.AugmentedBalancing))
```

| Constructor parameter | Default | Accepted values and meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| `balance` | `"double"` | `"none"`, `"unit"`, `"time"`, or `"double"`; selects the optimized weight dimensions |
| `unit_target` | `"cohort"` | `"cohort"` for one donor vector per treatment cohort or `"individual"` for one vector per treated unit |
| `time_target` | `"all"` | `"all"` for one mean-post target or `"period"` for one target per post period |
| `balance_on` | `"raw"` | `"raw"` fits weights on $Y$; `"residual"` fits them on $Y-\hat m$ |
| `unit_loss` | `"ridge"` | `"ridge"` for SDID simplex ridge or `"penalized_scm"` for the R donor-distance loss |
| `unit_penalty` | `0.0001` | Nonnegative penalized-SCM distance coefficient |
| `zeta_omega` | `None` | Optional nonnegative unit-ridge scale; `None` uses the R data-dependent rule |
| `zeta_lambda` | `None` | Optional nonnegative time-ridge scale; `None` uses the R data-dependent rule |
| `max_iterations` | `1000` | Positive active-set iteration budget |

Use:

```python
model = cm.AugmentedBalancing(...)
model.fit(y, w, outcome_model=None)
```

- `y` is a finite balanced outcome matrix with units in rows and periods in columns.
- `w` is a same-shaped binary absorbing-treatment matrix.
- `outcome_model` is an optional same-shaped untreated-outcome surface fitted without treated post-treatment outcomes. If omitted, it is zero.

All three arrays must be two-dimensional. `y` and `outcome_model` must be finite. `w` must be binary and absorbing. Each treated cohort must have at least one pre-treatment period, and the panel must contain a never-treated donor. Invalid constructor choices, invalid arrays, unsupported treatment paths, and solver failures raise `ValueError`. `predict()`, `treatment_effect()`, and `summary()` raise `ValueError` before a successful fit.

### Counterfactual formula

Let $C$ be never-treated controls, $P$ be pre-treatment periods, and $\hat m$ be the supplied outcome model. Define residuals $R=Y-\hat m$. For treated unit $i$ and post period $t$,

$$
\widehat Y_{it}(0)
=
\hat m_{it}
+\sum_{j\in C}\hat\omega_jR_{jt}
+\sum_{s\in P}\hat\lambda_sR_{is}
-\sum_{j\in C}\sum_{s\in P}\hat\omega_j\hat\lambda_sR_{js}.
$$

The balance choice controls which weights are optimized:

| `balance` | Unit weights $\omega$ | Time weights $\lambda$ |
|---|---|---|
| `"none"` | Not used | Not used; returns $\hat m$ |
| `"unit"` | Optimized | Uniform over pre periods |
| `"time"` | Uniform over controls | Optimized |
| `"double"` | Optimized | Optimized |

With `balance="unit"`, the estimator retains the time correction and uses uniform pre-period weights.

### Targets

- `unit_target="cohort"` fits one donor vector to the treated-cohort mean.
- `unit_target="individual"` fits one donor vector per treated unit.
- `time_target="all"` fits one pre-period vector to the control post-period mean.
- `time_target="period"` fits one pre-period vector for each post period.

The R “individual double” row maps to `unit_target="individual", time_target="period"`.

### Weight-fitting data

- `balance_on="raw"` fits weights with $Y$.
- `balance_on="residual"` fits weights with $R=Y-\hat m$.

In both cases, the final augmentation formula is applied to residuals $R$. `balance_on` changes the weight-fitting problem, not the final algebra.

### Unit losses and penalties

`unit_loss="ridge"` implements the SDID simplex ridge problem with a profiled intercept. If `zeta_omega` and `zeta_lambda` are omitted, the R defaults are

$$
\zeta_\omega=(N_{\text{target}}T_{\text{post}})^{1/4}\hat\sigma,
\qquad
\zeta_\lambda=10^{-6}\hat\sigma,
$$

where $\hat\sigma$ is the sample SD of control first differences in the selected balancing data. For individual unit targets, $N_{\text{target}}=1$.

`unit_loss="penalized_scm"` implements `penSCM` from the R source. It standardizes the donor matrix by its sample SD and adds the linear donor-distance penalty. `unit_penalty=1e-4` is the R default. Time weights remain SDID ridge weights.

The internal active-set solver handles simplex boundary solutions directly. It can represent exact zero weights, unlike a softmax parameterization.

### R-frame map

| R frame | Python configuration |
|---|---|
| outcome | `balance="none"`, supply `outcome_model` |
| u-balance | `balance="unit"`, omit `outcome_model` |
| t-balance | `balance="time"`, omit `outcome_model` |
| d-balance | `balance="double"`, omit `outcome_model` |
| aug-u-balance | `balance="unit"`, supply `outcome_model` |
| aug-t-balance | `balance="time"`, supply `outcome_model` |
| aug-d-balance | `balance="double"`, supply `outcome_model` |
| residual variant | add `balance_on="residual"` |
| individual unit variant | add `unit_target="individual"` |
| individual time variant | add `time_target="period"` |
| individual double variant | set both individual target options |
| R ridge loss | `unit_loss="ridge"` |
| R penSCM loss | `unit_loss="penalized_scm"` |

### Fitted outputs

```{python}
example_panel = classic_factor(overlap=1.0, seed=91)
example_model = cm.AugmentedBalancing(
    balance="double",
    unit_target="individual",
    time_target="period",
    balance_on="residual",
)
example_model.fit(
    example_panel.outcome,
    example_panel.treatment,
    np.zeros_like(example_panel.outcome),
)
example_summary = example_model.summary()
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "key": sorted(example_summary),
        "type or shape": [
            np.asarray(example_summary[key]).shape
            if hasattr(example_summary[key], "shape")
            else type(example_summary[key]).__name__
            for key in sorted(example_summary)
        ],
    }
)
```

`predict()` returns the fitted counterfactual surface. `treatment_effect()` returns $Y-\widehat Y(0)$ for treated units. `summary()["att"]` is the simple mean over treated cells. Weight arrays include explicit target mappings:

- `target_units` and `target_cohorts` identify unit-weight rows;
- `time_target_periods` uses `-1` for an all-post target and a zero-based period for period-specific targets;
- `time_target_cohorts` identifies the cohort for each time-weight row; and
- `zeta_omega` and `zeta_lambda` report fitted ridge scales. `zeta_omega` is zero when penalized SCM is used.

| Method | Return contract |
|---|---|
| `fit(y, w, outcome_model=None)` | Fits in place and returns `None` |
| `predict()` | Full counterfactual array with the same shape as `y` |
| `treatment_effect()` | Full $Y-\widehat Y(0)$ array with the same shape as `y` |
| `summary()` | Dictionary with the ATT, surfaces, diagnostics, weights, targets, cohorts, and configuration |

## Reproduction workflow

The exact R summary is regenerated without the unavailable outcome packages:

```bash
Rscript scripts/export_r_slide_results.R
```

The Python Monte Carlo run is:

```bash
uv run python -m website.vignettes.balancing_support.run_balancing_experiments --replications 200 --workers 16
```

Add `--output-directory website/vignettes/results` to overwrite the vignette's
cached Python summaries. A normal documentation render reads those summaries
and does not rerun the 2,800 panel draws.

The runner stores every replication in `results/python_replications.csv`, then derives `results/python_rmse.csv`. The comparison table is rebuilt with:

```bash
uv run python -m website.vignettes.balancing_support.compare_r_python
```

Render the complete site and all executable documentation with:

```bash
uv sync --extra docs
uv run quarto render website
```

## Scope and limitations

- Same-panel parity tests the numerical estimator implementation. It does not test random-number-generator parity.
- The Monte Carlo comparison tests common probability laws with independent language-specific random streams. Differences are therefore evaluated with combined Monte Carlo standard errors.
- The Monte Carlo comparison covers all 398 displayed R/Python cells. FE, IFE, MCPanel, generalized synthetic control, and VAR also have same-panel R parity fixtures. ARIMA has a Monte Carlo check but no historical-`fable` same-panel fixture in this environment.
- The experiments compare point-estimator RMSE under a common-adoption design. They do not evaluate interval coverage, staggered adoption, or treatment-effect heterogeneity beyond the common linear post-treatment path.

## Conclusions

- Unit-only balancing is effective in several good-overlap and synthetic-control settings.
- No single balancing or outcome-model configuration is uniformly best.
- Double balancing materially reduces RMSE under poor factor-loading overlap and under persistent integrated dynamics.
- Individual unit and post-period targets can help, but they are different estimators and require many more weight fits.
- Outcome-model performance remains DGP-specific. The R and Python heatmaps show that `gsynth`, `ife`, `MCPanel`, `VAR`, and `arima` have different strengths. A horizontal-ridge result cannot stand in for those columns.

These conclusions rest on an exact same-panel R test, executable R DGP contracts, 200 successful draws in every Monte Carlo cell, and a between-language comparison scaled by combined Monte Carlo uncertainty.
